extracted.intended_audience: educated British public, policymakers, and readers concerned with the French Revolution (late-18th-century political readers)
extracted.subtask_description: A conservative political essay/pamphlet critiquing the French Revolution and arguing for the preservation of established manners, religion, and institutions; addressed to the British public and political class. The page sets out normative principles about law, morality, government, and social institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws should be supported by affections and manners
rubrics_metrics.description: There ought to be a system of manners in every nation, which a well-formed mind would be disposed to relish. To make us love our country, our country ought to be lovely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affections combined with manners act as supplements, correctives, and supports to law; institutions must be 'embodied in persons' to create love, veneration, admiration, or attachment. The precept from poetry ("Non satis est pulchra esse poemata, dulcia sunto") is invoked to argue that beauty and sweetness (affection) are needed alongside correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely solely on terror to support laws
rubrics_metrics.description: On the scheme of this barbarous philosophy... laws are to be supported only by their own terrors, and by the concern which each individual may find in them from his own private speculations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If laws are maintained only by fear, nothing remains to engage the affections of the commonwealth; such a reason which banishes the affections cannot fill their place, and institutions will fail to be embodied in persons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public affections and manners are necessary aids to law
rubrics_metrics.description: These public affections, combined with manners, are required sometimes as supplements, sometimes as correctives, always as aids to law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Law alone without social sentiments cannot sustain a civilized polity; manners and affections give permanence and internal motivation to obedience beyond fear of punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve ancient manners and opinions as a moral compass
rubrics_metrics.description: When ancient opinions and rules of life are taken away, the loss cannot possibly be estimated... From that moment we have no compass to govern us; nor can we know distinctly to what port we steer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Removing long-standing moral frameworks deprives a people of guidance; the author links manners and opinions to the flourishing of learning, commerce, and civilization, arguing their removal risks decay into barbarism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning should be an instructor, not aspire to be master
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning... would have been satisfied to continue the instructor, and not aspired to be the master!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If learning abandons its role as guardian and becomes the controlling political force, it will be debauched and ultimately 'cast into the mire'—the author warns against intellectuals overruling traditional social anchors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commerce and the arts depend on social protections like nobility and religion
rubrics_metrics.description: Even commerce, and trade, and manufacture... certainly grew under the same shade in which learning flourished. They too may decay with their natural protecting principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economic prosperity is presented as rooted in manners and religion; destroying those protections risks simultaneous economic and cultural decline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prejudice (longstanding customs) has practical value in forming habitual virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Prejudice renders a man's virtue his habit; and not a series of unconnected acts. Through just prejudice, his duty becomes a part of his nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inherited prejudices supply ready application in emergencies, engage the mind steadily, and give permanence to moral behavior; thus blind rejection of all prejudices is unwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government should not be treated like transient fashion
rubrics_metrics.description: They think that government may vary like modes of dress, and with as little ill effect: that there needs no principle of attachment, except a sense of present conveniency, to any constitution of the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author criticizes doctrines that justify rapid, fashion-like change in constitutions and warns that stable attachment beyond present convenience is necessary for political health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid justifying perfidy and murder by 'public benefit'
rubrics_metrics.description: Justifying perfidy and murder for public benefit, public benefit would soon become the pretext, and perfidy and murder the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolerance of criminal means on utilitarian grounds corrupts moral judgment, shortens the path to objectives, and promotes rapacity, malice, and revenge; once criminal means are tolerated they are soon preferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punishment of real tyrants should be grave, decorous, and dignified
rubrics_metrics.description: The punishment of real tyrants is a noble and awful act of justice; and it has with truth been said to be consolatory to the human mind. Justice is grave and decorous, and in its punishments rather seems to submit to a necessity, than to make a choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If vengeance is required, it should be administered with dignity and respect for the moral weight of justice, not with brutal triumphalism or degrading spectacle; the manner of punishment reflects on the cause of liberty and humanity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not degrade someone as a criminal and then entrust them with high office
rubrics_metrics.description: To degrade and insult a man as the worst of criminals, and afterwards to trust him in your highest concerns... is not consistent in reasoning, nor prudent in policy, nor safe in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political consistency and prudence demand coherence between condemnation and subsequent appointment; treating a person as culpable then restoring them to high trust undermines legitimacy and prudence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Before removing an established institution present a viable replacement
rubrics_metrics.description: Before we take from our establishment the natural human means of estimation, and give it up to contempt... we desire that some other may be presented to us in the place of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Removing institutions without offering a substitute risks creating a void that the mind will fill with pernicious or uncouth superstition; orderly reform requires a replacement ready to assume the role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion is the basis of civil society and should not be replaced by atheism
rubrics_metrics.description: We know... that religion is the basis of civil society, and the source of all good and of all comfort... We shall never be such fools as to call in an enemy to the substance of any system to remove its corruptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author insists that reforms should not invite atheism or infidelity as a remedy; religious belief is presented as essential to moral and civil order and to resisting social decay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatre (art) can be a superior school of moral sentiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Indeed the theatre is a better school of moral sentiments than churches, where the feelings of humanity are thus outraged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Through intuitive, empathetic response, theatre can teach moral distinctions more effectively than abstract doctrinal preaching; this is used as an argument against politically justifying crimes by calculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revolutions that destroy manners and opinions risk producing tyranny and moral decay
rubrics_metrics.description: The usurpation which... has destroyed ancient principles, will hold power by arts similar to those by which it has acquired it... Kings will be tyrants from policy, when subjects are rebels from principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The loss of ancient moral anchors leads to governments that sustain themselves by plots, preventive violence, and confiscation; the author predicts cycles of tyranny and social savagery without proper respect for inherited institutions.
